title: Understanding Transfer on Death Deed Issues (October 2026)
summary: TOD deeds skip probate but don't erase mortgages or liens. Learn about common transfer on death deed issues families face, updated October 2026.
body_markdown:
A transfer on death (TOD) deed names a beneficiary to receive real property at the owner's death, and a valid deed allows the property to pass outside of[probate](https://www.elayne.com/resources/probate-explained-what-happens-after-someone-dies-and-how-to-plan-ahead) . The deed does not remove a mortgage or lien, and it does not give the beneficiary authority over the rest of the estate. Whether the transfer is valid depends on state law and on how the deed was signed and recorded. This guide covers key topics for families and executors to be aware of, including: signing and recording defects, who has authority to act, a conflicting will, beneficiary death and joint ownership, mortgages and liens, post-death paperwork, inheritance mapping, and more.


**Key Takeaways**


- Signing or recording defects can invalidate a TOD deed. Requirements vary by state.
- In Texas, a will cannot revoke a TOD deed or change its named beneficiary.
- TOD deeds do not erase mortgages or liens, even when the property avoids probate.
- Beneficiaries may still need ownership filings and heir notices after a TOD transfer.


## What Is a Transfer on Death Deed?


A transfer on death deed, or TOD deed, names a beneficiary to receive an owner's real property interest at death. A[properly recorded TOD deed](https://texaslawhelp.org/article/transfer-on-death-deeds-todds) allows that interest to pass without probate when applicable legal requirements are met. During life, the owner retains ownership rights and can sell the property or use it as collateral for a loan.


Probate avoidance applies only to the property covered by the deed. Other estate assets may still require probate, depending on their ownership and whether they have valid beneficiary designations.

## 1. Signing and Recording Defects Can Prevent a Transfer


Missing signatures, improper signing, or late recording can prevent[a transfer on death (TOD) deed](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-is-a-transfer-on-death-deed-how-tod-deeds-help-you-skip-probate) from taking effect.


California provides an example:


- Rules effective January 1, 2022, require[signatures from two witnesses](https://saclaw.org/resource_library/transfer-on-death-tod-deed-naming-beneficiaries-and-revoking-tod-deeds/) .
- California's form requires recording[within 60 days](https://saclaw.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/form-tod-deed-1.pdf) after signing and notarization. If the deed is not recorded within that deadline, it does not transfer the property at death.


These requirements are not nationwide standards. Validity depends on the applicable state's signing and recording rules.


## 2. A Conflicting Will May Not Change the Deed


A will governs property passing through the estate; a transfer on death (TOD) deed transfers the covered interest separately. A later will does not necessarily change the deed’s beneficiary.


In Texas, a will cannot revoke a TOD deed. Revocation requires statutory formalities, including recording before the owner’s death.


## 3. Mortgages, Liens, and Creditor Claims Can Remain


A transfer on death (TOD) deed does not erase a mortgage, tax lien, or other enforceable interest attached to the property. In Texas, beneficiaries receive the property subject to interests existing at the owner's death. Debt attached to the home is different from personal liability for repayment. Further creditor exposure depends on state law.

## Comparison of Transfer on Death Deed Problems


Problem Possible Effect


Signing or recording defects Transfer may fail


Conflicting will Deed may control


Outstanding debts Property remains burdened


Post-death paperwork Incomplete ownership documentation


## How Elayne Supports Estate Organization After a TOD Transfer


An effective TOD deed may transfer a property outside probate. Authority to act, title documentation, and remaining estate obligations are separate questions.


[Elayne](https://www.elayne.com/company) offers estate organization, Verified Asset Search, inheritance mapping, and shared document access to help families understand how that property fits into the broader estate.


### Who has authority to act


A TOD deed and an estate rely on different sources of authority. The beneficiary named in a valid deed receives the property through the deed itself.[An executor](https://www.elayne.com/resources/what-does-an-executor-of-a-will-actually-do-a-complete-guide-to-executor-duties) or personal representative acts under a will and court-issued letters, and that authority covers the probate estate. In general, a personal representative does not control real property that passes by an effective TOD deed, although state law on creditor claims varies.


### How TOD records are organized with the rest of the estate


Elayne brings the records tied to a TOD transfer into one structured estate record. Those records can include the recorded deed, earlier ownership deeds, the death certificate, any will, and mortgage or lien statements. They sit beside bank accounts, insurance policies, debts, and other assets, so a TOD property appears as one part of the full estate instead of a separate file.


Signing and recording dates, the property's state, and information about deceased beneficiaries or joint owners can be kept with each document. Those details help give a professional the information needed to identify the rules that apply.


### How inheritance mapping treats TOD property


Inheritance mapping records who inherits and how each asset transfers. Each asset is categorized by the way it transfers: trust, TOD or payable on death designation, joint ownership, community property, or probate. A home passing under a TOD deed falls in the TOD category, and a bank account with no named beneficiary falls in the probate category. The result is a picture of which assets follow which path.

Verified Asset Search is Elayne's financial discovery capability. It uses credentialed access that goes beyond public records to surface real property and deed records, along with life insurance, unclaimed property, vehicle records, and accounts a family may not know exist.


### Shared access and professional review


Authorized family members, executors, and advisors work from one shared dashboard with role-based permissions. For example, attorneys can access documents and progress alongside family members. Each person sees what the assigned role permits, and the shared record shows which documents and steps are complete.


## FAQ


### What records can beneficiaries organize in Elayne before a professional reviews their TOD deed?


Useful records include the recorded TOD deed, prior ownership deeds, the death certificate, any will, and mortgage or lien statements. Signing and recording dates, the property's state, and information about deceased beneficiaries or joint owners can help a professional identify the applicable rules. Shared document access lets authorized family members and professionals work from the same records.


### Can beneficiaries use Elayne when their TOD property bypasses probate but other assets do not?


Yes. A TOD property and probate assets can follow separate transfer paths within the same estate. Elayne's inheritance mapping helps organize those paths.


### Does a TOD beneficiary need to know about the deed or consent to it?


In states that follow the Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act, a TOD deed is effective without notice to the beneficiary, acceptance by the beneficiary, or payment of consideration. During the owner's life, the beneficiary holds no ownership interest. The owner can sell, mortgage, or revoke the deed without the beneficiary's consent.


Other states set their own rules, and some use different names for the same tool, such as beneficiary deed. Because a beneficiary may first learn of a deed after the owner's death, locating property records is often an early step for families. Elayne's Verified Asset Search helps surface real property and deed records.


### What happens if the TOD beneficiary dies before the owner?


The outcome depends on the deed's wording and on state law. A deed can name a contingent beneficiary to take the property if the first beneficiary dies first. Some states supply a substitute, such as the beneficiary's descendants, when the deed is silent, and other states do not.


If no named beneficiary is able to take the property, it generally returns to the owner's estate and passes under the will or state intestacy rules, which typically involves probate. Elayne keeps information about deceased beneficiaries with the deed documents so a professional can review them. Which rules apply is a legal question for a local attorney or a court.


### What steps commonly follow a TOD transfer after the owner dies?


Steps vary by state and county. They commonly involve a certified death certificate and a document recorded with the county recorder or land records office, such as an affidavit confirming the owner's death. Some states also require notice to the owner's heirs. A title company may ask for these records before a sale or refinance.


Ownership carries the ongoing costs of the property, including property taxes and insurance. Reassessment rules and transfer tax filings differ by jurisdiction.


Elayne holds the recorded deed, death certificate, and mortgage or lien statements in one shared record, and each person sees what their assigned role permits.


### Does a TOD deed override a surviving joint owner's rights?


In states that follow the Uniform Real Property Transfer on Death Act, a surviving joint owner's right of survivorship takes priority. A TOD deed signed by one joint owner takes effect only if that owner is the last surviving owner. If the other joint owner outlives the signer, the survivor holds the property by survivorship. Other states may apply different rules.


Co-owned property can involve several transfer paths in one estate. Elayne's inheritance mapping categorizes each asset by how it transfers: trust, TOD or payable on death designation, joint ownership, community property, or probate.
